prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, reaching accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight first-round statements, the case I made has been tested by seven colleagues and none has found a flaw in the science. The invention is bounded and statable in one sentence: trapping many neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, so that the lattice light shifts both clock levels equally, removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors while allowing parallel interrogation for stability. The outcome is measured, not promised: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, reproduced by independent national laboratories and compared routinely. The consequences are already realised in part, in tests of fundamental constants and relativity and in relativistic geodesy. The credit is clean, with Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability, and it fits the three-person limit without forced exclusions. In answer to the chair, I propose the citation wording above, which names magic-wavelength lattice trapping and the 1e-18 performance and deliberately does not say optical clocks or frequency standards in general, so that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize are neither claimed nor slighted.
statement.case_against: The reservation that every B057 supporter shares is still the strongest: precision metrology sits next to two recent prizes, and the line between the lattice concept and the comb and ion-clock work is sharp in the physics but less sharp in the public reading. Ye's programme is bound up with comb-linked comparison, which is the part most exposed to the 2005 overlap, and the citation should rest on the lattice and the measured accuracy, not on comparison technology. Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups are outside the credit, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Against this, B053 has a real case as a new organising principle with a mature field, and I do not dismiss Eriksson's argument; the unresolved Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit and the 2016 overlap are what keep it behind B057 for me.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B053 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new classification of insulators and a theory-plus-experiment pairing, accepts B057 as a good outcome, and says B057 has a clearer discovery-plus-invention profile.
responses.response: I take the organising-principle argument seriously, and I agree the field is mature and widely confirmed. My difficulty is the credit, not the physics. A three-name prize for B053 has to explain why the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D ARPES work by Hasan fall outside it, and the 2016 prize on topological phases presses on the novelty of the Z2 classification. B057 has no comparable internal tension in who did the decisive step. Your own acceptance of B057 as a good outcome is useful: if the committee judges the credit for B053 unresolved, I understand you would not obstruct the clocks, and I would support B053 as the strong next candidate.

responses.point: Mehlig raises timing relative to the redefinition of the second, notes Ido and Kimble as precedents for lattice trapping, and in round 1 kept B005 as a future prize because five names compete for three places.
responses.response: I agree with your handling of B005 and have kept it only as an alternative; with five names for three places and an unsettled split between the proposal and the decisive experiments, it cannot compete this year. On timing, my answer to the chair is that the redefinition is neither a condition nor a reason to wait: the scientific achievement is complete when independent clocks agree at 1e-18, and the redefinition is a later metrological decision. On Ido and Kimble, I accept your caution and would not word the citation as the first idea of trapping in a lattice but as the invention and development of the magic-wavelength lattice clock, which is what Katori demonstrated and Ye brought to its limits.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube (B054) to B057 as the stronger case, still values B054 as opening a new observational window, and worries that lattice clocks could be read as a family of incremental advances.
responses.response: I welcome your move and I accept that B054 is a major achievement. On the incremental reading, the test I apply is whether the measurement capability changed in kind. A neutral-atom lattice clock with many atoms interrogated in parallel at 1e-18 changed what could be measured, and it did so through one concept and not a series of tweaks, which is what separates it from a refinement. For B054 I share your hesitation about isolating three names from a large collaboration and from AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, so I treat it as a later candidate, not a rival this year.

responses.point: Olsson agrees with the two-name credit but says the ion-clock question should not be waved away as a footnote and that the citation should name the lattice clock specifically, resisting a third name.
responses.response: That is fair, and I have taken it on board in the proposed citation, which names magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and does not use optical clocks generically. I agree that the ion work is thereby neither claimed nor slighted, and I agree with resisting a third name: the unrepresented groups made real contributions, but the same is true of almost every candidate on this list, and no member has put forward a documented decisive contribution that would displace either Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B057, agrees that the citation must be tight around lattice trapping because Ye's comb-linked programme is the most exposed to the 2005 overlap, and discloses a professional interest in B021.
responses.response: I agree on the exposure of the comb-linked part of Ye's work. I would answer it by resting Ye's credit on what he did with the strontium lattice clock, namely systematic evaluation and the record accuracy and stability, which is lattice physics, and not on the comb itself. That keeps both laureates tied to a single invention. I also appreciate your disclosure on B021; since it is not a preferred configuration for anyone this year, it does not bear on the outcome.

responses.point: Danielsson agrees on science and credit, argues the discovery side (constancy of nature's parameters) makes this a physics prize, and reads timing as timely but not urgent.
responses.response: I accept your framing on timing and I think it is more careful than my 'timely or overdue'; I do not want the committee to rush for the sake of the redefinition. I agree that the tests of the constancy of fundamental parameters give the prize its physics character and would let the citation text say 'accuracy and stability' while the supporting rationale carries the tests of constants and relativity.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues outside atomic physics accept the separation from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes as sufficient, now that the citation is drawn around the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether a third name is needed for fair attribution; I currently see no documented decisive contribution that would displace Katori or Ye, but my view rests on my own field's reading of the record.
Whether the committee reads precision measurement as equal in weight to a discovery-type prize such as B053 when both are scientifically sound.
Whether the hardening of the SI second redefinition timeline will change how the prize is read, although I do not treat it as bearing on the merits.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during my doctoral period, and Hall was recognised in 2005 for frequency-comb work on which optical clocks build. It documents no tie to Katori or Ye, and I know of none. In reply to the chair, I judge the connection to be a distant scientific lineage and not a personal or institutional interest in the outcome, and I would accept the committee's decision if it thinks recusal is warranted. I also work in laser spectroscopy and precision optics and in quantum memories, so my field is close to B057 and to B005, which I flag as disciplinary closeness. Lindroth and I share this atomic-physics lens, and I agree with her that the case should be tested by colleagues outside AMO.
